claims.text: An active-learning moment tensor potential with on-the-fly ab initio corrections will significantly improve reference–target phase-space overlap in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The proposed MTP will reduce free-energy integration error by a factor of 2–3 relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
Equimolar Nb–Ni–Ti–Zr–Co is an example of a multicomponent high-entropy alloy to which the intervention applies.
The intervention applies to both solid and ab initio liquid states near the alloy's high melting point.
The MTP will be iteratively updated during high-temperature molecular dynamics using periodic ab initio DFT corrections.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 3000–3500 K.
The applicable compositions are equimolar HEAs exhibiting a bcc solid and a liquid phase.
Continuous on-the-fly refinement enables the MTP to capture transient local atomic environments that static potentials miss.
Continuous on-the-fly refinement enables the MTP to capture rare configuration events that static potentials miss.
DFT corrections in the active-learning loop cause the MTP to adjust to newly encountered atomic configurations.
Dynamic adjustment makes the MTP represent the ab initio potential-energy surface of the high-temperature liquid more accurately.
Improved representation of the liquid potential-energy surface minimizes thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
A successful calculation will yield a crystalline–liquid free-energy difference with uncertainty below 5 meV/atom.
TOR-TILD's static EAM references do not capture the full range of atomic configurations.
The limited configurational coverage of TOR-TILD's static EAM references causes larger TI path mismatches and free-energy uncertainties.
The effectiveness of the intervention may be limited by the computational cost of DFT corrections.
Insufficient active-learning update frequency may fail to capture rare but important configurations.
The magnitude of TI-path-mismatch reduction may vary with simulation parameters and convergence criteria.
Failure to reduce TI integration error by at least a factor of 2 relative to TOR-TILD's EAM falsifies the hypothesis.
Failure to converge the interphase free-energy difference within 5 meV/atom falsifies the hypothesis.
